title: The Five Garments of the First Man and the Two Garments of the Departing Soul
arc: The teaching grounds the question of how a soul departs the body — clothed either in light or in darkness — in the cosmogonic descent of the First Man, whose Living Fire received a wound while his four companion garments (wind, water, light, air) served as helpers and were exchanged in their stations; from this primal wounding-and-exchange the teaching draws its rule that every kingdom acts from one single principle, so that what agrees with the Light is exalted in the garment of life-light and what agrees with Darkness perishes under the hand of the opposing kingdom.
reading:
This chapter answers a doctrinal question raised by its title — how a man comes forth from the body wearing either a garment of light or a garment of darkness — by reaching back to the cosmogonic moment when the First Man went out against the Enemy. What the soul wears at the body's gate is not arbitrary; it is determined by the same law that governed the original engagement of Light and Darkness, and the surviving fragments lay out that law in two movements.

The first movement is cosmogonic. Divine Truth descending into the natural — the First Man — went forth against the King of Darkness clothed, that is, bearing his five-fold completeness as garments around him. Within that outermost garment was the Living Fire (divine love in its active form), and the Living Fire did the decisive work: it quenched the foolishness and arrogance of the Enemy, the disordered burning of self-love that had spread itself out as the Enemy's expanse. One alone of the divine sons sufficed for that work. But because the Living Fire engaged the Darkness directly, it received a wound in its body — the standard Manichaean image for Divine Truth crucified in the natural, the Living Soul taking on tribulation in matter. The Mother of Life answers this wounding by sending the four further garments — that of the wind, that of the water, that of the light, and that of the air — as helpers around the Living Fire. Their function is to surround it so that the corruption it has taken on may be cut off, and so that the wound may be borne not by Fire alone but distributed through the four. They share the destruction with him; they too receive a wound, and so all five Sons of the First Man pass through the same engagement.

Yet the engagement is not symmetric. The teaching is careful: the power of the Enemy did not actually join with them; the Darkness did not enter into them; the Enemy's burning was not able to encircle them. The wound is real, but the substance of Light is not absorbed by Darkness. One alone of the four — the air — remained without wound, and precisely this unwounded one is then stripped naked of its garment and its power. The garment is given to another in its place, so that in this garment of the Living Air the four may prevail and be joined together, and so become for the saved a garment of life-light. The cosmogonic point here is that the divine garments are interchangeable in their stations, but their substance returns home; what is given up below is given again above. The Living Air, stripped, becomes the very form in which the four are reunited as the new clothing of life.

The second movement draws the doctrinal consequence. The Greatness of the Light lives in mutual conjunction forever; none of its members transgresses the commandment and the parangelia which the brother (the Beloved of Lights, in his emanative role) has given — namely, not to be like the Darkness. The Enemy stands on the opposite side of this same axiom: he is one whose entire being is a single practice in his principle, he himself alone; and his kingdom too is the same principle, she herself alone. Each kingdom is what it is wholly; neither is mixed in itself; the mingling lies only in the natural arena where their garments are exchanged. From this the teaching derives the rule of the soul's departure. The powers of light have left their Deep behind them and come up after the one whom they have appointed for themselves, because of the single practice that exists in them all. By that ascent they scatter the Darkness and humble its powers; by the might of that first Light they reproduce, in the manner proper to it, what the corrupt kingdom does in this cosmos.

The closing rule is therefore exact and reciprocal. As long as a soul's mysteries — that is, the inner correspondences and confirmed practices of its life — agree with the kingdom of Light, they do honor to her, they receive glory according to what is established, and they are exalted exceedingly above the opposing kingdom that rose against her. But the kingdom whose fellow-mysteries agreed with Darkness lies under the necessity of perishing in that kingdom, of being humbled, and of coming under the hand of the kingdom that stands against her. This is what it means to come from the body wearing one garment or the other. The garment is not an accident put on at the moment of death; it is the accumulated agreement of the soul's mysteries with one of the two single principles, woven through the whole life. At the body's gate the soul appears clothed in whichever set of garments her practice has actually confirmed — either in the four-fold garment of the living elements that the Mother of Life recomposed around the Living Fire, or in the foul garment of the Darkness which has only its own single practice to give.

The arc of the teaching is thus a single argument from cosmogony to eschatology: because Light and Darkness each act from one whole principle, and because the First Man's garments were exchanged but never absorbed, every soul leaves the body wearing what it has joined itself to, and the law that governed the original wounding of the Living Fire is the same law that exalts or humbles the soul at its departure.
